title: Rituals are leaky boats (1.2)
hookLine: the Mundaka praises the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats, and both statements sit side by side in the same chapter
carry: rites earn a heaven that ends; moksha isn't earned
tomorrow: go to a teacher, fuel in hand
last: BRAHMAN SPINS THE WORLD FROM ITSELF.

lines: NOW CROSS AN OCEAN IN IT.
cards: A rowboat can be a perfectly good boat. It'll take you around the lake, out to the dock, across to the picnic spot. Now try to cross an ocean in it.
Nothing about the boat has changed. What changed is where you're trying to go. The second section of the Mundaka does something bold with that idea.
It's talking about the great fire rites of the Vedas. First, it honors them. Then it calls them boats, and tells you what kind.

teach.b: The section opens with a clear yes. This is the truth, it says: the rites the sages saw in the sacred verses are spread out in many ways. Practice them faithfully.
This is your path to the world of good deeds.

Then it describes the fire offering in loving detail, the seven flickering tongues of flame, each with a name: the black one, the terrible, the swift as thought, the deep red, the smoky, the sparkling, the one of every shape.
Then the turn. Plava hy ete adridha yajnarupah.

Unsteady, indeed, are these boats, the eighteen forms of sacrifice. Fools who praise them as the highest good go again and again to old age and death. Thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind.
They enjoy the heaven their good works earned, and when it runs out, they come back down. So which is it? Are the rites true, or leaky?
The Mundaka says both, on purpose. The rites really do what they promise: they earn a good world. But a good world is still a world that ends.
They're boats for the lake, not the ocean.

teach.h: THE UNMADE ISN'T WON BY THE MADE.
teach.b: Then the line that explains the whole section: the uncreated is not won by what is made. Nasty akritah kritena. That's a big Hindu teaching.
Heaven, svarga, is earned by good deeds, and it runs out.
Moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death, isn't a thing anyone can make or buy. Different schools weighed this differently. The Mimamsa tradition held ritual itself as the heart of the Veda.
Vedanta teachers read this passage as the turn toward knowledge. Others keep the rites and the inner search side by side.

how: Hindu households keep daily and seasonal rites, from lighting a lamp to fire offerings (homa), and Vedanta teachers explain this passage as a lesson about what rites can reach, not a call to stop them.

o: an unsteady boat that can't cross the ocean
a rite that wins the deathless for good
a fire offering with seven tongues of flame

games.q: inside the passage — tap the pairs.
p: true: the path to good worlds
the blind led by the blind
those who think rites are all
not won by what is made

s: the Mundaka says Vedic rites are false and useless
it calls them true, then says they're unsteady boats for crossing beyond death.
the text names seven tongues of the sacred fire
the black one, the terrible, the swift as thought, and four more.
the heaven earned by rites lasts forever, in this text
when the merit runs out, they come back down.

games.q: you've done the fire rites faithfully all your life. the Mundaka says they're true. what does it say they can't do?
o: they can't earn any good world.
they can't carry you across to the uncreated.
they can't be done by householders.
games.why: they earn a good world that ends. the unmade is not won by what is made: nasty akritah kritena.

practice: Think of one thing you do faithfully, a ritual or routine that's good for you, and honor it for a breath: it works, it carries you.
Then ask gently where it's carrying you, and whether there's somewhere it can't go, without answering quickly. Then let the question go and sit for a moment, nothing made, nothing earned.

wordCard.voice: Plava, an unsteady boat. The Mundaka honors the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats: they earn good worlds, but the uncreated isn't won by what's made.

orig.note: Sanskrit plava, a boat or float: 'unsteady boats are these forms of sacrifice', Mundaka 1.2.7.

carryVoice: Your line: rites earn a heaven that ends; moksha isn't earned. That's week fifty-nine: prana carries the rest, breath is the self's shadow, the seer in sleep, satya, two knowledges, the spider, and the leaky boats. Day four hundred thirteen.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.1–1.2.12 (the rites are true; seven tongues; blind led by the blind; the uncreated)
